blocks.text: E.3.3. What Remains: Three Embodiment Gaps
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Co-training absorbs the visual appearance of the robot, but it does not by itself close the embodiment gap. Three gaps remain, in sensing, actuation, and environment, and each requires a deliberate design choice. We quantify them in turn (Tab. 16) and then ablate the choices that close them.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: • Sensing gap. The two embodiments observe the scene through cameras with substantially different fields of view (Tab. 16 and Fig. 42). UMI pairs a wide-FOV head camera with fisheye wrist cameras of about 180∘(OAK), whereas YAM uses a standard-FOV top camera and pinhole wrist cameras of 78 × 63∘
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: (RealSense D405). The two wrist cameras also differ in orientation and in where they sit relative to the
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: fingers. As a result, even the stereographic re-projection of the wrist fisheye used in pretraining places the scene 74 to 94 px from where YAM’s camera shows it at 320 × 240 (Fig. 43). The lens centers are also 4.9 cm apart, so a re-projection can align the scene but not the fingers, which stay smaller in the UMI view than in YAM’s. Beyond geometry, the UMI frames show the operator’s arms and the handheld gripper, whereas YAM’s frames show its own arms and gripper (Fig. 42). • Actuation gap. Beyond sensing, the two embodiments differ in how actions relate to states and in the space in which actions are expressed (Tab. 16). First is action versus state. A UMI demonstration only records the pose the handheld gripper reached, so action and state coincide and the data assume zero tracking error. On YAM, the action is the command of a teleoperation leader arm and the state is where the follower arrives, and the two differ because the follower is a low-stiffness position-controlled arm (brushless motors with 40:1 shoulder and 10:1 wrist reductions under a PD controller with joint stiffness
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: from 80 down to 10 N m/rad). It lags the leader by about four frames (133 ms at 30 Hz) and settles at a load-dependent offset from the command. YAM data thus teach the policy to command ahead of, and offset from, the observed state, whereas UMI data teach it to command the state itself. Second is the control space. UMI acts in end-effector space, with gripper widths as labels. YAM’s action row holds the end-effector pose and width plus the six joint positions of each arm, 32 dimensions in all. Handheld data supply only the 20 end-effector dimensions, and the 12 joint dimensions have no counterpart. Even the shared dimensions use different conventions: UMI poses refer to a wrist frame at the gripper motor center

blocks.text: Ablation 1: shared versus separate action head. GR00T 2 shares its diffusion transformer across embodiments but keeps one row of action-encoder, state-encoder, and action-decoder weights per embodiment. The sharedhead arm re-expresses UMI in YAM’s semantics and places it on YAM’s row: grasp-site poses, absolute widths normalized by the 85.55 mm full opening, the first 20 of YAM’s 32 action dimensions, and YAM’s normalization statistics. The separate-head arm keeps UMI on the row it was pretrained on, with wrist-frame relative poses, relative widths in millimetres, and its own statistics. The separate arm therefore changes the action representation as well as the head, so the comparison is not a single-variable change. The two arms trade embodiment grounding against skill coverage, and the results in Tab. 17 split along that line. The shared head is clearly stronger on Toy Dumptruck Assembly (60% versus 10%) and Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing (86% versus 64%), whereas the separate head is slightly better on NIST Board Disassembly (60% versus 50%,
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: progress 93 versus 86). The NIST margin is concentrated in the hex-nut subtask, which the separate head completes in 7 of 10 trials and the shared head in 5 of 10. This is also the subtask on which the demonstrations are most specific: the UMI demonstrators slide the nut off its post without rotating the wrist, and the YAM co-training data do not contain this way of removing a nut. With the shared head, UMI actions are decoded by the same weights as the YAM data, so the decoder’s prior follows YAM’s motion statistics, and a strategy that
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: appears only in the demonstrations is reproduced less reliably. The separate head keeps UMI on the row it was pretrained on and preserves the demonstrators’ strategy. The same mechanism explains the reverse outcome on the other two tasks: where the demonstrated motions are ones the YAM data already perform, placing UMI on YAM’s row grounds the task evidence directly in YAM’s action statistics and controller, whereas the separate head must rely on the transformer to map YAM observations onto a row it has never seen paired with them. The shared head is therefore the better default, while the separate head helps only where the demonstrations rely on a motion strategy that the co-training data do not share.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 2: wrist-view alignment. We re-render the native UMI fisheye (≈180∘) as a virtual standard-FOV pinhole camera at the same optical center that imitates YAM’s 78 × 63∘wrist view (Tab. 16 and Fig. 43): a 202.96 px focal length at 320 × 240 (76.5 × 61.2∘), pitched about 27.1∘down, with rotation and focal length fitted in Isaac Sim on 112 same-scene UMI/YAM render pairs. On held-out pairs, the scene error is 8 px for objects closer than 30 cm and 11 px beyond, versus 74 and 94 px for the stereographic view, and the grasp zone is resolved at 12.5 rather than 6.9 px/cm for the raw fisheye. Identical maps back-fill the training data and run at deployment. We stress that this alignment is approximate. It matches the field of view and the viewing direction of YAM’s wrist camera, but not the lens, the stereo baseline, the offset of the optical center from the gripper, or the appearance of the arm and fingers in the frame, and the residual discrepancy is visible in Fig. 43. We compare three training views for the UMI wrist cameras: the stereographic view used in pretraining, the YAM-aligned view, and a random choice between the two on every training sample. Only the aligned view transfers on the two long-horizon tasks (Tab. 17). With the stereographic view, end-to-end success is 0% on both long-horizon tasks, and 46% of the items are sorted on Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing. The random mixture recovers 60% on tossing but still 0% on the long-horizon tasks, while the aligned view reaches 60%, 50%, and 86%. The progress scores tell a more specific story. They fall only moderately without alignment (96 to 79 on Toy Dumptruck Assembly, 86 to 76 on NIST Board Disassembly), so the policy still performs
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: most steps. What it loses is the precision steps, in which the gripper must meet a screw hole or a nut within a few millimetres. A view mismatch moves the grasp zone in the image and changes its pixel scale (12.5 versus 6.9 px/cm), which corrupts exactly the image-to-action mapping those steps depend on, while leaving coarse transport intact. The random mixture helps only on tossing (60% versus 46%), where coarse transport suffices, and not on the precision steps, because it asks the policy to be invariant to a viewpoint change that is informative for those steps. The policy averages over two geometries and is sharp in neither. We draw two conclusions. First, the video model absorbs the appearance gap, since human arms and a handheld gripper in training versus robot arms in deployment do not prevent transfer, but it does not absorb a geometric gap. Second, the geometry need only be roughly matched: coarse agreement in field of view and viewing direction is sufficient to recover most of the transfer, which makes the method practical for new target robots whose wrist cameras are known only from a datasheet.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 3: amount of UMI data. The UMI demonstrations are the only source of the target task, so their number bounds how much task evidence post-training can draw on. We shrink each cohort to about half and a quarter of its episodes at a fixed 0.6 : 0.4 UMI : YAM sampling ratio (Tab. 17). The three tasks degrade very differently. Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing is nearly flat (86%, 84%, 70%): it is a short-horizon dynamic skill with one decisive event, and 20 episodes already cover it. Toy Dumptruck Assembly degrades gradually in end-to-end success (60%, 30%, 10%) while its progress score stays high (96, 92, 81), the signature of a long horizon in which small per-step losses compound multiplicatively. Notably, the policy trained on only 20 demonstrations still completes the full four-stage assembly end to end in 1 of 10 trials and 81% of its individual steps, on a robot that has never been teleoperated for the task. NIST Board Disassembly collapses at the first halving (50% to 0%), and the substage table shows why: the nut subtask goes from 5 of 10 to 0 of 10 while the other four subtasks barely move. The data requirement of a task is therefore set not by its length but by its hardest subskill, the one with the least support in both the pretraining and the co-training data. That subskill is the first to disappear as demonstrations are removed, and in a sequential task its loss zeroes the end-to-end rate. In practice, 41 to 75 handheld demonstrations sufficed for every task here, and half of that sufficed whenever
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: the task contained no such rare subskill.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 4: UMI-10K in pretraining. The main result (Tab. 4) already shows that starting from a checkpoint pretrained without UMI data reduces transfer success to 20% and 0% on the long-horizon tasks and the share of conveyor items sorted to 34%. We repeat the row in Tab. 17 and examine what pretraining contributes. Both models see the same post-training data and the same number of steps, so the difference lies entirely in what the pretrained weights already encode. The checkpoint without UMI also differs in pretraining length, robot mixture, and small model details (Sec. E.2), so not all of the gap need come from UMI data. We identify two contributions. First, with UMI-10 data in pretraining, UMI’s observation domain, a handheld gripper and human arms seen through fisheye wrist views, is already in-distribution for the video backbone, so post-training does not have to learn to see the demonstrations. Second, and more important for transfer, pretraining on UMI alongside YAM and the other robot corpora aligns UMI’s actions with the other embodiments inside the shared transformer: the model has already learned that a UMI grasp and a YAM grasp are the same event. Post-training then only needs to attach task evidence to an alignment that exists, whereas without UMI in pretraining the same 41 to 75 episodes must simultaneously teach the observation domain, bind it to YAM’s action semantics, and teach the task. The few-shot budget is spent on the embodiment rather than on the task. The progress scores are consistent with this reading. Without UMI pretraining the policy still performs most coarse steps (84 and 65), so it does learn the task structure. It fails at the precision steps, where an imprecise embodiment alignment turns into a missed hole or a dropped part. UMI data in cross-embodiment pretraining are thus not a convenience but the mechanism that makes a few dozen demonstrations sufficient.

blocks.text: E.4. DexUMI Exoskeleton Hardware

The GEAR DexUMI exoskeleton (NVIDIA GEAR Team, 2026) replicates the kinematics of the target robot hand (XHAND1 Pro-U) joint for joint and reproduces its fingertip and palm contact surfaces, which keeps the visual

and physical gap to the robot small for policy training. It is also designed for wearability, so that operators can comfortably collect high-quality data across long, dexterous tasks. Compared with the original DexUMI, it offers the following improvements:

• More degrees of freedom. The exoskeleton captures 16 degrees of freedom, using 20 joints of which four pairs are coupled. • Higher precision and durability. Machined parts give higher precision and durability. • No over-constraint, better tracking and wearability. Removing non-essential contact surfaces and adopting a remote-center-of-motion (RCM) linkage resolves the over-constraint of the original structure. The structure flexes less, which improves tracking precision and wearability. • Daisy-chained encoders. The joint encoders are daisy-chained, which simplifies cable management. • Left and right hands. Both left- and right-hand versions are available, enabling bimanual tasks.

Remote-center-of-motion joints. Matching the robot hand’s abduction/adduction (AB/AD) and flexion joints is a packaging problem, since those joint centers lie where the operator’s finger is. We replicate them with an RCM linkage that creates a virtual joint at the robot hand’s joint center without placing hardware in the operator’s workspace (Fig. 44a). The RCM is a parallel four-bar linkage. To avoid over-constraining it, only two of the four holes at the top joint are used. Leaving the other two unused reduces binding from manufacturing tolerances and keeps motion smooth.

Thumb. The thumb linkages use a “kicked-out” geometry that preserves the robot hand’s thumb kinematics while clearing space for the operator’s own thumb, so its range of motion is unobstructed during dexterous manipulation (Fig. 44b).

Rigid, compact joints. Every joint is supported on both sides to prevent deflection and improve measurement precision. Custom pins keep joint bulk low while forming secure connections, and a variant with a direct keying interface mates to the joint encoders, reducing backlash and improving sensor accuracy (Fig. 45a).

Figure 44: GEAR DexUMI kinematic design. (a) A remote-center-of-motion linkage places a virtual joint at the robot hand’s AB/AD and flexion joint centers. (b) The kicked-out thumb linkage keeps the robot hand’s thumb kinematics while clearing the operator’s thumb.

Contact surfaces and camera. The fingertip and palm tactile-sensor contact surfaces match the robot hand’s, and the fingertip geometry is reproduced on the exoskeleton to reduce the visual gap between human collection and robot execution (Fig. 45b). Non-essential contact surfaces are removed to improve wearability. The camera mounting angle and alignment are carried over to the robot hand’s mount, so the collected images match the deployed field of view (Fig. 45c). Finally, the chassis is anodized green so that a color threshold can segment it for the masked-video augmentation (Sec. E.6).

Sensing. The exoskeleton fingertips report force in the robot hand’s own tactile format: five fingertip sensors with two pads and three force axes each, 30 channels per hand. Per hand, an iPhone tracks a wrist frame 12.6 cm from its lens, which a per-arm hand-eye calibration maps onto the robot, and the same 640 × 400, 45 fps wrist and head cameras serve collection and deployment.
E.5. DexUMI Post-Training Recipe

For the DexUMI results of Sec. B.3, we post-train the 2B GR00T 2 model from the GR00T 2 pretraining checkpoint for 60,000 steps at a learning rate of 3 × 10−5, with 224 × 320 images from the wrist cameras and, optionally, the head camera. The policy predicts 40-step action chunks at stride 2 on the 45 fps data: relative end-effector poses for each arm and, for each hand, either absolute joint positions with joint torques or offset joint positions in their place (Eqs. (1) and (3)).
E.6. DexUMI WAM-Native Inpainting

GR00T 2 addresses the visual gap between the exoskeleton and the robot hand inside training rather than by editing video: it corrupts the exoskeleton region so that the model cannot rely on exoskeleton-specific appearance. By WAM-native inpainting we mean this in-model treatment, in place of offline video editing. Our earlier pipeline, following the original DexUMI (Xu et al., 2025), filmed each demonstration replayed on a real robot hand, segmented the exoskeleton from manually picked keypoints, inpainted it with ProPainter, and composited the robot hand back in, at the cost of robot time, manual input, and GPU-heavy segmentation and inpainting.

Exoskeleton masks. We segment the green regions in every camera video with HSV color bands, morphological cleanup, and a ±2-frame temporal majority vote, and store each mask as a lossless binary video beside its RGB stream.

Figure 45: GEAR DexUMI joints, contact surfaces, and camera. (a) Double-sided joint support and a custom pin with a direct keying interface to the joint encoder. (b) Fingertip and palm contact surfaces replicate the robot hand’s tactile sensors. (c) The camera mount matches the robot hand’s mounting angle and alignment.

F. RL Post-Training

Pretraining equips GR00T 2 with broad visual and motor priors, but reliable real-world manipulation often requires adaptation to precise alignment, contact dynamics, and physical interaction. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), enabling policies to improve through
robot experience and task-level feedback.

Applying RL to GR00T 2 introduces unique challenges. Unlike action-only policies, GR00T 2 jointly generates actions and predicted visual futures through iterative denoising. Policy optimization must therefore accommodate joint video-action computation while enabling effective exploration. Furthermore, physical interaction is expensive, requiring efficient algorithms and infrastructure to make iterative post-training practical.

We address these challenges through three complementary components. First, we develop direct GR00T 2 posttraining methods, including GRPO-based optimization (Shao et al., 2024) and self-imitation from successful RL exploration, alongside residual RL for localized corrections (Sec. F.1). Second, we leverage AutoRL, an autonomous research system that discovers and improves RL post-training algorithms through closed-loop experimentation in simulation (Sec. F.2). Third, we develop scalable infrastructure that coordinates robot interaction, training, and evaluation while preserving experience and minimizing iteration overhead (Sec. F.3). We demonstrate these capabilities on four real-world precision manipulation tasks (Sec. F.4). We also investigate RL post-training through interaction with a learned neural simulator. We adapt DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026) to recorded policy rollouts, then demonstrate that GR00T 2 can improve through world-model-based RL (Sec. F.5).
F.1. RL-Based Adaptation of World-Action Models
blocks.section: F.1. RL-Based Adaptation of World-Action Models

blocks.text: We investigate two complementary strategies for adapting GR00T 2. Direct GR00T 2 post-training updates the pretrained model through RL or self-imitation, while residual RL freezes GR00T 2 and learns a lightweight corrective policy. The former improves the underlying generative policy, whereas the latter targets precisioncritical stages where GR00T 2 already produces approximately correct behaviors.

blocks.text: Stochastic Exploration with CPS. To enable exploration and likelihood-based policy optimization (Liu et al., 2025; Lei et al., 2026), we replace GR00T 2’s deterministic Euler action updates with Coefficients-Preserving Sampling (CPS) (Wang and Yu, 2025) during rollout. Noise is injected only into the action denoising process. Video denoising remains deterministic given its initial latent, while video features continue to condition action generation.

blocks.text: F.2.1. Autonomous Experimentation Harness
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Each AutoRL discovery round follows four stages. First, the agent analyzes previous experiments, diagnostic metrics, and failure modes to identify bottlenecks. Second, it proposes up to four mutually orthogonal hypotheses, each specifying an isolated mechanism, expected outcome, and falsification criterion. A critic filters out redundant or insufficiently testable proposals. Third, valid hypotheses are implemented in independent branches, locally tested, and submitted for cluster training and evaluation. Finally, candidates are compared with the current best baseline and promoted only when improvements exceed a predefined margin. At most one candidate is promoted per round, while rejected hypotheses remain available as negative evidence.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: This harness enables systematic exploration of algorithmic modifications beyond conventional hyperparameter tuning.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: F.2.2. Discovering RL Recipes
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: AutoRL starts from a standard PPO implementation and iteratively improves the post-training recipe through successive experiments (Fig. 47). Below, we summarize the eight changes marked in Fig. 47 by the component they affect, each with the best gain over the base model reached after it.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Weight anchoring and longer rollouts. Early runs showed the actor drifting rapidly from the pretrained weights, losing existing skills before any useful RL gradient appeared, and rollouts on the long-horizon RoboCasa365 tasks ending before the task could be completed. The agent added an 𝐿2 penalty toward the pretrained weights and extended the rollout horizon. Together these give 1.6 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Replacing the critic (group-relative baseline). The critic’s explained variance stayed near zero, so its advantages were noise. More capacity and warm-up did not help. The agent removed it in favor of a grouprelative baseline in the style of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), the ℎ𝑔= 0 case of Eq. (12), and extended the horizon further. Cumulative gain: 3.5 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Shaping the return (stage progress). Six long-horizon composite tasks still did not move: with binary success every attempt in a group failed identically, leaving no relative signal. For these simulation experiments, the agent introduced stage-progress returns in [0, 1], assigning partial credit according to the furthest subgoal milestone reached. The real-robot experiments instead use binary task-success returns, as defined in Sec. F.1.1. Cumulative gain: 4.1 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Balancing long and short tasks. Long tasks were trained with an execution horizon of 16 but scored with 8, and training them at 8 as well raised the cumulative gain to 5.0 percentage points. An advantage weight of 2.5 on long tasks crowded out the short ones, and lowering it to 1.5 gave 6.5 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Less noisy advantages (grouping and stage credit). Task difficulty varied widely within a group, which made the group-relative advantages noisy. Grouping rollouts by initial scene and seed raised the cumulative gain to 7.5 percentage points. Failures often came after some stages had already been completed, so the agent added stage-aware credit within each episode, which gave 7.9 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: Remembering each context (persistent baseline). Progress rewards do not help contexts the policy already solves every time or never advances at all. Their groups stay uniform and a current-group baseline gives them zero advantage, and on RoboCasa365 such contexts are most of the data. The agent gave every context a memory of its past returns, an exponential moving average across rounds (Eq. (14)), folded into the leave-oneout baseline as a small number of pseudo-observations (Eq. (12)). This baseline retains a learning signal for uniform-outcome groups when their current returns differ from past performance. The same context statistics also guide rollout allocation away from consistently solved contexts. Cumulative gain: 10.0 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: These experiments demonstrate how AutoRL systematically discovers effective post-training strategies: stabilizing policy optimization, replacing an uninformative critic, balancing long and short tasks, improving credit assignment, and keeping a learning signal alive on saturated and unsolved tasks. The resulting algorithm forms the foundation of our direct GR00T 2 post-training approach, which we further adapt to GR00T 2’s joint video-action architecture and real-world robot interaction. As demonstrated in Sec. F.4, this approach achieves substantial improvements on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
blocks.section: F.2. Automated Discovery of RL Post-Training Algorithms

blocks.text: F.3. Online RL Post-Training Infrastructure

Real-robot RL requires repeated coordination among data collection, reward annotation, policy optimization, and evaluation. These stages have different resource requirements and execution rates, while physical interaction and scene resets constrain collection throughput. We develop shared infrastructure that supports heterogeneous learning algorithms, reduces iteration overhead, and preserves experience across failures (Fig. 48).

Shared Experience Buffer. Our infrastructure uses a shared experience buffer backed by Lance (Pace et al., 2025). Experience records are constructed incrementally as collection, scoring, and batch preparation produce their outputs. Workers can selectively access relevant fields, while training updates use pinned table versions to ensure stable inputs (Lance Contributors, 2026). Common record identities and policy provenance associate observations, rewards, and updates, and algorithm-defined schemas support different post-training methods within the same data infrastructure.

Resource-Efficient Execution. Collection, training, and evaluation use independently configurable resource pools. Compatible GPU resources can be reassigned according to workload dependencies, accommodating both on-policy and off-policy learning. Incremental uploads and prefetching overlap collection, data transfer, scoring, decoding, and training preparation, reducing idle time between iterations.

Stateful Recovery. Physical experience is expensive to reproduce, making robustness to interrupted training essential. Our infrastructure retains experience data and feedback alongside model and optimizer checkpoints. Recovery distinguishes experience already reflected in a restored checkpoint, data associated with discarded updates, and unused data. Compatible experience can subsequently be reused for resumed training or offline learning, reducing redundant physical interaction. This complements prior work on distributed RL execution and durable robot experience data (Yu et al., 2026a; Zang et al., 2026a,b; Wang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c).
Execution Efficiency. We evaluate infrastructure efficiency in simulation and real-robot training.

In RoboCasa365 GRPO, rollout and training alternate on a shared 40-GPU pool while evaluation retains 40 GPUs. This reduces total allocation from 120 to 80 GPUs and enables evaluation to overlap training. Across eight rounds and nine evaluations, execution time decreases from 14.1 to 8.8 hours, corresponding to approximately 1.6× improvement in update throughput.

For single-robot GRPO (Tab. 18), experience pipelining and trainer-ready records reduce upload and conversion time from approximately 50 minutes to one minute, while transferring only tuned weights reduces policy download time from approximately 30 minutes to one minute. Total iteration time decreases from between 140 and 160 minutes to between 62 and 72 minutes, yielding approximately 2.2× iteration throughput. Incremental uploads overlap data transfer with physical collection, leaving only a short data-handling delay at the end of each round. F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: We evaluate three complementary post-training approaches on four real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating how GR00T 2 improves through RL-based learning and targeted policy adaptation.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: Tasks. Our evaluation includes four precision manipulation tasks (Fig. 49). In fixed-pipe fittings, the robot grasps a threaded tee fitting, aligns it with a horizontally mounted pipe, engages the threads, and completes one full turn. This is the Fixed-Pipe Fittings task of Tab. 1a, but each RL trial starts from a fitting pose that the post-trained policy struggles with. In finger placement, the robot inserts two 3 mm pins on a gripper finger into matching holes on a fixed base, requiring accurate position and yaw alignment.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: In cable insertion, the robot inserts an Ethernet connector into a designated network-switch port, with success determined by network-link connectivity. In charger insertion, the robot inserts a two-prong charger into a specified outlet within a 2 × 6 grid. These tasks involve tight geometric tolerances, partial occlusion, and contact-sensitive execution.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: Evaluation Protocol. All evaluated methods build on the same SFT-initialized GR00T 2 checkpoint, either as an initialization or as a frozen base. GRPO directly updates GR00T 2 using both successful and failed
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: trajectories. Self-imitation reuses successful GRPO rollouts without additional collection. Residual RL instead learns a separate controller on top of the frozen base, using human-assisted training experience.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: For each task, evaluations use the same target distribution, reset conditions, and time limits, with no human intervention during evaluation. Trials are independent of training rollouts, and we report per-task success rates. An episode is considered a failure if misalignment prevents the policy from recovering or if the insertion exceeds the time limit.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: Real-World Results. Direct RL on GR00T 2 improves precision manipulation. GRPO increases success rates on all four tasks (Fig. 5), raising fixed-pipe fittings from 66% to 86%, finger placement from 58% to 72%, cable insertion from 76% to 92%, and charger insertion from 40% to 94%. With 50 trials per task, the gains on charger insertion and fixed-pipe fittings are significant at the 5% level (two-sided Fisher exact test), whereas those on cable insertion (38 to 46 successes) and finger placement (29 to 36) are not conclusive at this sample size.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: Self-imitation consolidates successful RL exploration. Self-imitation reaches 88% on fixed-pipe fittings, 98% on finger placement, 94% on cable insertion, and 96% on charger insertion, matching or exceeding GRPO on all four tasks. The gain is most pronounced on finger placement, where success rises from 72% to 98%.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: These results highlight the potential of combining RL exploration with supervised policy optimization. RL discovers successful behaviors through interaction, while self-imitation consolidates them under a stable supervised objective. This offers a complementary route to improving GR00T 2 beyond direct policy-gradient optimization.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: Residual RL enables targeted adaptation without updating GR00T 2. Residual RL reaches 76% on fixed-pipe fittings, 84% on finger placement, 82% on cable insertion, and 70% on charger insertion, with clear gains over supervised post-training on finger placement and charger insertion. These results show that lightweight corrective controllers can improve precision execution while leaving the pretrained GR00T 2 intact.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: These experiments show that direct RL, self-imitation, and residual RL can improve GR00T 2’s precision manipulation through complementary forms of post-training.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: The preceding experiments improve policies through physical interaction. We next investigate a complementary source of training experience: interaction with a learned environment constructed from recorded policy rollouts.
blocks.section: F.4. Precision Manipulation through RL Post-Training

blocks.text: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: In neural-simulation RL, the policy interacts with a learned world model in place of the physical environment. This changes how training experience is generated while retaining reward-based optimization of the pretrained world-action policy.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We use DreamDojo (Gao et al., 2026), initialized from pretrained video priors, to turn recorded robot interactions into a learning environment. Successful and failed attempts provide supervision for task-specific adaptation. A pretrained GR00T 2 policy can then collect further training experience through interaction with the adapted model. Task rollouts are still required to construct this environment, while subsequent policy-learning rollouts are generated in neural simulation.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: To support policy learning, the model’s predictions must provide usable inputs to GR00T 2 throughout an episode. We provide multi-view camera predictions, align them with executed action chunks, and approximate proprioceptive inputs using action targets. We also maintain visual history across successive world-model calls. We first describe world-model construction and the closed-loop policy interface, including support for long-horizon interaction. We then present the experimental setup, reward modeling and policy optimization, and results in RoboLab and on real-world tasks.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Training Data and Task Adaptation. We first mid-train DreamDojo on multi-view episodes, then adapt the resulting model to downstream tasks. The bimanual YAM corpus contains 8,310 four-view episodes from policy
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: rollouts and DAgger collection, including failed attempts and recovery. These episodes total approximately 226.8 hours at 30 Hz. The DROID source corpus contains 57,773 episodes, approximately 273 hours at 15 Hz, with three synchronized camera views and recorded joint and gripper actions.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We tile synchronized camera views into one video canvas so that the model predicts them jointly using DreamDojo’s existing video backbone and causal variational autoencoder (VAE). YAM uses a 2 × 2 layout at 480 × 640 pixels. DROID concatenates three 180 × 320 views horizontally and pads the canvas vertically to 192 × 960 pixels.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Video and action sampling are aligned separately. For YAM, we downsample video from 30 to 15 Hz while retaining fourteen-dimensional actions at 30 Hz. Each window contains five conditioning frames and twelve future frames, paired with 24 future actions. DROID video and eight-dimensional actions both remain at 15 Hz, and each window contains five conditioning frames and sixteen future frames. We precompute and cache VAE latents, which are the compressed video representations used by the world model. We sample temporally aligned training windows from this cache, avoiding repeated encoding of the same recorded videos.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Task adaptation. We adapt the mid-trained world model to the scenes and action distributions encountered by the target policy. Successful and failed rollouts provide supervision on the states reached during execution, allowing the model to learn task-relevant visual changes and action effects. We fine-tune the model on these rollouts using the multi-view representation and temporal alignment used during policy interaction. Recorded robot actions and world-model inputs use consistent action coordinates and normalization.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Closed-Loop Simulation Interface. To collect experience for policy optimization, we alternate GR00T 2 action prediction with world-model prediction throughout a task episode. A rollout starts from recorded multi-view observations. GR00T 2 predicts an action sequence, and the world model predicts the camera observations resulting from its executed prefix. These predicted images become the policy’s next visual input, allowing GR00T 2 to respond to the consequences of its own actions. Repeating this interaction produces a trajectory for reward evaluation and policy learning.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: At interaction round 𝑟, GR00T 2 samples an action plan from the current observation and task instruction. Let 𝐴𝑟denote its executed prefix of 𝐻actions and 𝐶𝑟the world model’s conditioning latents. Initially, 𝐶0 is obtained by encoding five recorded video frames into two latent frames. The mapping 𝑔converts actions into the world model’s action coordinates and normalization. Future latents and the next conditioning history are then given by

blocks.text: 𝐹𝑟∼𝑝𝜑(· | 𝐶𝑟, 𝑔(𝐴𝑟)),

blocks.text: 𝐶𝑟+1 = Tail2([𝐶𝑟, 𝐹𝑟]).
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Here, Tail2 retains the final two latent frames of the concatenated conditioning and predicted sequence. After decoding, we remove the overlapping conditioning prefix and append the newly predicted images to the policy’s visual history. The views and historical frames required by GR00T 2 form its next observation, closing the interaction loop.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: The rollout preserves the video-action alignment used during training. For YAM, the world model predicts twelve new video frames at 15 Hz for 24 native actions at 30 Hz. For DROID/RoboLab, it predicts sixteen frames for sixteen actions, both at 15 Hz. We query the policy again after executing this action prefix and truncate the final round at the task horizon.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We exclude the five-frame conditioning prefix from the images returned to the policy. RoboLab decodes the complete latent window at each round. YAM retains the causal decoder cache and decodes only new latents after the first round. This decoder cache is separate from the latent history passed to the world model. For policies requiring proprioception, we initialize the state input from the recorded reset state. At each later policy query, we use the last executed action target as an approximation of the current robot state.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Long-Horizon Prediction. Policy learning requires multiple rounds of interaction, whereas the world model is trained on short video windows. We therefore generate successive segments autoregressively. After the first segment, the model conditions on its own predictions rather than recorded observations. Errors in this history can affect subsequent predictions and policy decisions.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: For the DROID-derived model used in RoboLab, we perturb recorded conditioning latents during training to expose the model to imperfect visual histories, while keeping recorded future latents as prediction targets. For a clean conditioning tensor 𝐶, we use
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation
F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: The noise strength 𝜎is sampled from 0, 0.0245, 0.0480, and 0.0925 with probabilities 0.2, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.2, respectively. We also explored replacing recorded history with a model-generated preceding segment, with gradients stopped through that history. These preliminary trials showed no clear additional benefit over noise augmentation, which we retain in the final training recipe.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: At rollout time, we pass the final two predicted latent frames to the next world-model segment as its conditioning history. This avoids decoding and re-encoding images to construct that history. We still decode predicted latents into images for GR00T 2: the world model carries its history in latent space, while the policy receives camera observations in pixel space.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Experimental Setup. Starting from SFT, GRPO updates GR00T 2 through interaction with the learned environment, while the world model and learned success detector remain fixed. Native RoboLab evaluation and real-world execution test whether these updates improve behavior outside the learned environment.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We collect rollouts from the initial GR00T 2 policy, retaining successful and failed attempts for world-model adaptation and reward supervision. The study covers ten RoboLab tasks and four families of physical manipulation: peg insertion, test-tube insertion into a specified rack hole, bun placement on yellow and white cups, and hardware sorting with nine instructions. Hardware sorting tests whether the policy selects the requested target object and destination from three target object categories and three colored trays in the presence of distractors. Fig. 52 illustrates the physical task setups.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: World-model adaptation uses 300 physical rollouts for each insertion task and each of the two bun-placement tasks, and approximately 300 rollouts in total for hardware sorting. The insertion and hardware tasks share a jointly adapted world model, while a separate model is adapted for bun placement. For RoboLab, we adapt one shared world model using 450 training trajectories per task across 64 tasks, with 50 trajectories per task held out. Joint policy RL uses ten tasks from this collection. Each RL run starts from its SFT baseline and keeps the world model and reward model fixed. RoboLab reward supervision uses 450 training and 50 validation trajectories per task. The test-tube success detector uses a separate set of 600 training and 120 validation videos labeled for insertion and release in the designated rack hole.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Reward Modeling and Policy Optimization. Sparse rewards. Dense progress rewards are difficult to obtain consistently across manipulation tasks and expensive to annotate. They can also introduce reward hacking when a policy increases a proxy score without completing the requested goal. We therefore use sparse task-completion rewards, learning a binary success detector rather than a continuous progress score.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We train compact success detectors based on VideoMAE (Tong et al., 2022) to provide rewards during RL. For physical videos, a vision-language model (VLM) proposes outcome labels and supporting visual evidence, and targeted human review resolves ambiguous cases. These offline labels supervise the compact detectors, avoiding VLM queries during policy learning. For hardware sorting only, annotated world-model rollouts augment the recorded videos to cover observations encountered in neural simulation. The other reward models use recorded task data.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Success is defined by the requested instruction: choosing the wrong object or destination is a negative outcome.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We use task-specific detectors, including instruction-specific outputs for joint hardware sorting. RoboLab provides native success labels, while physical-task labels use recorded outcomes and reviewed visual evidence. The detector and its task-specific decision rule remain fixed during RL. Final policy evaluation uses native RoboLab outcomes and physical execution, independently of the learned reward model.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Policy optimization. We apply the clipped transition-level policy optimization principle of Sec. F.1.1 to interaction with a fixed learned environment. We collect groups of attempts from the same recorded reset context and score them with the learned success detector. The neural-simulation experiments use Flow-SDE (Liu et al., 2025) for stochastic action denoising, while the physical-RL recipe uses CPS. Both provide tractable transition densities for likelihood-ratio updates.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: We optimize a clipped likelihood-ratio objective on selected action-denoising transitions. For each selected transition, we store the sampled latent input and output, denoising index, conditioning inputs, and behaviorpolicy probability. During optimization, we replay the same transition and recompute its probability under the current parameters with gradients enabled. The sampled transition and noise schedule remain fixed, so the likelihood ratio compares the two policies on the same sampled event.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Consistent replay is necessary because numerical differences can produce an apparent policy change before any update. We disable dropout, preserve positional-encoding precision, and check rollout and replay logprobabilities under unchanged weights before the first optimizer update. Activation checkpointing reduces memory use during backpropagation through the joint world-action model described in Sec. F.1.1. The likelihood ratio scores the selected action transition, with no separate video-likelihood objective or learned critic. In the physical-task recipe, we compute the actor loss using actions up to and including the first chunk in which success is confirmed. Later actions are excluded.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Policy Improvement in RoboLab. We evaluate task success using native RoboLab outcomes, independently of the learned world model and reward model. Fig. 50 compares the SFT policy with the policy obtained by joint RL from that initialization. Each policy is evaluated for 500 episodes per task, or 5,000 episodes in total, using matched observation and action settings and full task horizons. Mean success increases from 51.32% to 70.88%, a gain of 19.56 percentage points.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Batch and group size. Sparse rewards connect exploration to optimization: a larger group can reveal a return difference that a smaller group misses. In RoboLab, we compare (𝐵, 𝐺) = (512, 8) and (1536, 24), where 𝐵is the number of trajectories collected per round and 𝐺the number of attempts per reset group. Both recipes collect 64 groups and perform four optimizer updates per round.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Fig. 51(a) tracks DreamDojo rollout success and native RoboLab success at twelve policy checkpoints, including SFT. Native RoboLab success reaches 71% in evaluations of 100 episodes per policy. The separate final evaluation uses 5,000 episodes per policy and shows an increase from 51.32% to 70.88%. DreamDojo success is measured by the learned reward on training rollouts, whereas RoboLab evaluation uses native task outcomes. Because the sampling procedures and horizons differ, these curves track learning within each setting rather than measure simulator calibration.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Fig. 51(b) compares eleven matched collection budgets through 67,584 trajectories. The larger combined batch/group configuration has higher native RoboLab success at ten budgets, and its success rate is 11.1 percentage points higher on average across the eleven budgets. At the final budget, success is 71% versus 54%, a 17-point difference. At 24,576 trajectories, the rates are 68% and 47%, respectively.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: These single-run results favor the larger combined recipe. They also differ in optimization and reset layout: at the final budget, the smaller recipe has made 528 optimizer updates and the larger one 176. Late continuation of the smaller recipe additionally removed a numerical lower log-ratio bound. These differences limit attribution to either size parameter, and one run per configuration does not establish stability across independent runs.

blocks.text: Discussion. These results demonstrate policy improvement using experience generated by a world model adapted to an initial policy’s rollouts. GR00T 2 learns in this environment and is evaluated in RoboLab and on real-world robots. The current pipeline still requires task-rollout collection and task-specific world-model adaptation. Reusing the learned environment across new tasks and repeating the full world-model and policy improvement cycle remain directions for future work.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Our experiments focus on individual manipulation skills that serve as building blocks for more complex robot behavior. These skills can be integrated into agentic execution (Sec. G.1), where high-level orchestration, progress monitoring, and recovery coordinate actions across longer task horizons. RL-based adaptation and agentic execution therefore provide complementary mechanisms for improving robot reliability, from finegrained physical interactions to long-horizon task completion.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: Our longer-term goal is to develop scalable post-training methods that enable world-action models to improve consistently through real-world experience, extending their capabilities to increasingly challenging manipulation tasks.
blocks.section: F.5. Reinforcement Learning with Neural Simulation

blocks.text: G. Agentic GR00T 2

Pretraining and post-training equip GR00T 2 with increasingly capable manipulation skills, but robust longhorizon execution requires more than a strong underlying policy. Complex tasks involve multiple stages, task-level decisions, and unexpected failures that are difficult to resolve through continuous policy execution alone. Language instructions can also leave important aspects of task intent underspecified, such as which object to manipulate or where to place it.

We explore two complementary approaches to agentic manipulation. First, agentic skill composition and recovery integrates GR00T 2 with CaP, enabling higher-level agents to compose manipulation skills, monitor execution, and recover from unexpected failures (Sec. G.1). Second, steerable world-action generation exposes GR00T 2’s learned capabilities through the WAM API, allowing agents to guide and compose robot behaviors using visual targets (Sec. G.2). Together, these approaches enable higher-level reasoning agents to leverage GR00T 2 for complex, long-horizon manipulation.
G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Even after post-training, long-horizon manipulation remains vulnerable to compounding errors and unforeseen states (Ross et al., 2011). We introduce an agentic execution framework in which a frontier multimodal coding agent serves as System 2 (S2), composing GR00T 2 with CaP tools while monitoring task progress and recovering from failures. The agent verifies each intervention before resuming execution, without requiring GR00T 2 to learn every contingency.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The same framework supports complementary execution strategies. In simulation, we use ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) to discover task-level programs that call GR00T 2 as a manipulation tool, and each task runs either its program or GR00T 2 alone as the default executor, whichever succeeds more often on development seeds. On physical robots, where GR00T 2 is already capable of handling most manipulation, it remains the default controller. In both settings, S2 provides monitoring and CaP-based recovery. The key distinction is what executes between interventions.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Agentic Runtime Architecture. The runtime exposes GR00T 2 execution, robot observations, and CaP primitives through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). S2 uses these tools in an observe-reason-act-verify loop (Fig. 6).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The wam_act tool executes GR00T 2 with a task prompt and returns execution feedback. The agent can access camera observations and robot state through dedicated observation tools and adjust GR00T 2’s language prompt during execution if needed. The stop_wam tool terminates GR00T 2 execution when a recovery action requires control. CaP action primitives issue end-effector and gripper commands through inverse kinematics and motion planning, while observation primitives use vision foundation models for information such as object localization and pose estimation. CaP programs compose these primitives into executable skills that can be added at test time without retraining GR00T 2. A single control worker coordinates actuation so that GR00T 2 and CaP do not issue conflicting robot commands.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The agent receives an operating guide (AGENTS.md), skill documentation, and task context describing stages, success criteria, and known failure modes. It checks observations and tool feedback for stalled progress or errors, then invokes a recovery action when needed. Recovery may involve regrasping a dropped part, reorienting a component, or returning the robot to a valid configuration before execution resumes.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Program and Skill Acquisition. ASPIRE learns the executable behaviors used alongside GR00T 2, but the scope differs by setting. In simulation, it discovers task-level CaP programs that compose GR00T 2 calls with perception, geometric reasoning, and manipulation primitives. During online execution, S2 may reuse or adapt code from these programs for recovery. On physical robots, ASPIRE instead acquires targeted CaP skills, either through direct robot interaction or through CaP sim-to-real transfer, in which skills are learned in simulation and adapted to real-world conditions (Sec. J.2.4).
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Simulation Evaluation. We evaluate on RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) and RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026a) using four configurations: SFT, SFT + RL, SFT + Agent, and SFT + RL + Agent. For agentic execution, ASPIRE discovers programs using 15 development seeds per task. On 30 development seeds, including those 15, we then run each task’s program and GR00T 2 alone, and make whichever succeeds more often the task’s default executor, keeping the program on ties. With the SFT checkpoint, this selects GR00T 2 for 23 of the 50 RoboCasa365 tasks and 12 of the 54 RoboDojo task configurations. S2 starts every episode with the default executor, monitors it, and invokes online CaP recovery when needed. We test on 50 held-out seeds per task on both benchmarks (25 each for the standard and randomized variants of RoboDojo’s generalization tasks), disjoint from the development seeds.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: With SFT alone, GR00T 2 achieves the highest success rate of any non-agentic policy on both the RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo leaderboards (Sec. J.3 and Tab. 19). Memory- and reasoning-based tasks and high-precision manipulation still leave room for improvement.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: RL post-training with AutoRL (Sec. F.2) mainly improves precision, raising RoboDojo Precision success from 40.5% to 53.7%, and lifts average success from 67.2% to 72.4% on RoboCasa365 and from 35.2% to 40.8% on RoboDojo layout bank 0 (Tab. 19). Agentic execution helps most on memory- and reasoning-focused tasks: ASPIRE programs and S2 raise success on RoboCasa365 Composite-Unseen tasks from 38.2% to 69.5% and on RoboDojo Memory tasks from 36.0% to 93.7%. Overall, it brings average success to 81.8% on RoboCasa365 and 72.3% on RoboDojo, and combining it with RL gives the best results on both benchmarks. Compared with the top entries of both public leaderboards, including agentic submissions, SFT + RL + Agent ranks first on RoboCasa365 (88.0% vs. 85.6% for HexaShell 1.5) and on RoboDojo, where we evaluate layout bank 0 only (75.8% vs. 68.9% for Q0-Preview) (Tab. 19).

blocks.text: To characterize online recovery in the SFT + Agent setting, we split episodes by whether S2 intervened (Tab. 20). S2 rarely lets a failure through: of the episodes it leaves untouched, only 29 of 1,320 fail on RoboDojo and 20 of 1,512 on RoboCasa365. Of the episodes it intervenes in, 24% succeed on RoboDojo (188 of 773) and 56% on RoboCasa365 (553 of 988). Fig. 53 shows one rescue and one failed recovery.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: A manual review of failed SFT + Agent episodes on both benchmarks (Fig. 54) shows that most failures fall into two groups: the recovery requires manipulation too precise for S2 to perform with motion-planning tools (38% on RoboCasa365, 39% on RoboDojo), or the episode reaches a state that can no longer be recovered,

blocks.text: Real-World Long-Horizon Manipulation. We evaluate agentic execution with GR00T 2 as the default controller on multi-stage assembly and repeated precision insertion, examining how CaP recovery complements policy post-training.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Multi-stage assembly. We consider Toy Plane, Toy Tractor, and Hot Wheels assembly (Fig. 55). To stress-test robustness, each episode begins by dumping parts onto the table, producing clutter and varied object poses. The robot must assemble the parts in order, use a toy drill, and recover from execution errors. We compare SFT, SFT + DAgger (Ross et al., 2011), and SFT + DAgger + Agent.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: The Toy Plane task assembles a fuselage, two wings, and two screws using a toy drill. It requires seating and fastening the bottom wing, turning the airplane over, and fastening the top wing, with bimanual handovers and accurate screw-hole alignment. Success requires both wings fastened and the drill set down. The Toy Tractor task mounts and fastens two small front wheels and two large rear wheels, turning the body over between sides and returning it upright at the end. The Hot Wheels task mounts the correct front and rear wheels and installs a correctly oriented hood, fastening the components with a drill.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Fig. 7a reports the results. DAgger improves Toy Plane Assembly, Toy Tractor Assembly, and Hot Wheels Assembly success from 69%, 51%, and 23% to 84%, 71%, and 78%, respectively. Adding agentic execution further increases success to 98%, 97%, and 97%. This improvement reflects the ability of S2 to detect and repair local execution failures while preserving GR00T 2’s learned manipulation capabilities. Because every trial starts from parts dumped at random, these success rates measure robustness to unseen starting configurations and are not directly comparable with the post-training benchmark (Tab. 1a), whose trials start from arranged layouts. For Hot Wheels Assembly, for example, the benchmark reports 85% success from its fixed layout.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: For multi-cable insertion, five Ethernet (RJ45) cables stand upright beside a network switch. The robot must connect them in a fixed order to five designated ports. CaP first localizes all twelve candidate port faces using SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025) and camera depth, then grasps each connector and transports it along a collision-free path to a pre-insertion pose. GR00T 2 performs the insertion, and S2 checks for an Ethernet link and verifies that the connector occupies the assigned port. If insertion stalls or exceeds 60 s, CaP retracts the connector and prepares another attempt, allowing up to three attempts per port. S2 can stop retries early if the connector has rotated in the gripper. The episode succeeds only if all five connectors are inserted, a setting that compounds insertion errors and introduces occlusion from previously inserted cables.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: For multi-charger insertion, a human specifies five target outlets by pointing to them in order among twelve visually identical outlets arranged as a 2 × 6 grid. S2 grounds the gestures to individual outlets, with SAM 3 providing an independent interpretation. CaP grasps and transports each charger from its holder to the selected pre-insertion pose, and GR00T 2 performs the insertion. S2 checks whether the corresponding letter of an illuminated sign turns on and verifies the final target. Stalled or timed-out attempts can trigger CaP recovery, with at most three attempts per outlet and a 90 s limit per attempt. The task requires both accurate grounding of nonverbal instructions and precise insertion as the scene grows more cluttered.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Fig. 7b shows that RL post-training improves long-horizon insertion reliability within the same agentic system. For multi-cable insertion, success rises from 12/20 to 19/20, and for multi-charger insertion, it rises from 2/20 to 20/20. The gains highlight the value of RL-trained precision skills within long-horizon agentic execution.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

Late intervention accounts for three failures (one tractor, two Hot Wheels): GR00T 2 mounts a small wheel on an incorrect rear hub before S2 stops it, and the available CaP skills cannot reliably reverse the operation. blocks.text: On repeated insertion, SFT + RL + Agent fails in only one of the 40 evaluated episodes, due to a timeout during multi-cable insertion. SAM 3 yields an imprecise connector grasp, leading to an offset pre-insertion pose. Although the RL-trained policy moves toward the port, alignment recovery requires small exploratory motions while maintaining forward pressure and supporting the connector against gravity, and the attempt exceeds the 60 s limit. This case illustrates how residual pose errors can still make recovery too slow under a fixed execution budget.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: Together, these evaluations demonstrate two complementary forms of agentic execution. In simulation, ASPIREgenerated programs provide the task structure that direct GR00T 2 execution may lack, with online CaP recovery addressing unexpected states. In the real world, GR00T 2 performs most manipulation directly, while S2 detects failures and invokes targeted CaP skills, including skills acquired through CaP sim-to-real transfer. Both strategies extend GR00T 2’s capabilities through programmable recovery without requiring every contingency to be absorbed into the foundation policy itself.
blocks.section: G.1. Agentic Skill Composition and Recovery with Code-as-Policy

blocks.text: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Agentic skill composition and recovery (Sec. G.1) integrates GR00T 2 with external CaP programs and skills, whereas agentic steering keeps GR00T 2 as the only controller and lets the agent shape its behavior through the WAM API. We first describe the three parts of visual steering, in which the agent adds visual guidance to its language instructions: the interface, the agent loop, and the mid-training of GR00T 2. We then evaluate visual steering on short- and long-horizon benchmarks on YAM and Dexter.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Visual Guidance Interface. The interface separates what and where from how. For each step, the agent names the acting arm and gives a grasp point and a release point as pixel coordinates in the image of one scene camera (Tab. 21), while GR00T 2 determines the grasp pose, the approach, and all motion in between. We observed
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

Only the acting arm is marked, and only on the current frame of the scene camera. Alongside the markers, GR00T 2 receives the agent’s per-step instruction, which names the

blocks.text: Agent Loop. The agent loop has three layers. System 2 is the agent, which plans the steps and judges whether each step is done and what comes next. System 1 is GR00T 2, which executes the current step from the agent’s instruction and points. The harness is the rule-based program between them, which passes the agent’s instruction and points to GR00T 2 and decides when to query the agent. We use GPT-6 Astra as the agent, zero-shot and with one conversation per episode. At the start of an episode, it receives the task instruction and the images from all of the policy’s cameras, plans the steps, and returns the acting arm and the two points for the first step. The harness queries the agent again when an arm releases an object, when a fast vision-language model, used as a completion checker reports the step done, or after 45 s without a step end. The agent then decides whether to advance to the next step, redo the current one, replan the remaining steps, or finish.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Mid-Training for Visual Guidance. Following the points requires mid-training, because pretraining never shows GR00T 2 markers on its observations. We generate the point labels automatically from existing demonstrations by detecting grasp and release events for each arm (Tab. 21). If an arm’s next event is a grasp, its grasp marker is placed at that grasp and its release marker at the following release. If the arm already holds an object, the grasp marker stays at the preceding grasp and the release marker is placed at the next release. Each marker is the end-effector position at the event, projected into the scene camera. Markers are drawn for the arm that acts next, and an arm is never marked alone while the other arm is the one that acts next, so an unmarked arm next to a marked one should not act, as at evaluation. Each sample is conditioned on its annotated sub-task instruction, or on the task instruction where none exists.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Each point-conditioned checkpoint is mid-trained from the pretrained GR00T 2 checkpoint for 20k steps with AdamW (learning rate 5 × 10−5, warmup-stable-decay schedule). For each, we also train a languageonly checkpoint on the same data, cameras, schedule, and compute, without markers, which serves as the language-only baseline in the evaluation on YAM and on Dexter trash sorting.

blocks.text: Evaluation Settings. Each real-robot benchmark compares three settings, named as in Fig. 8. GR00T 2 is a language-only checkpoint given the original task instruction. GR00T 2 + Agent (language) is the same checkpoint given the agent’s per-step instructions, from the same agent loop with a prompt that omits the points. GR00T 2 + Agent (language + visual) is a point-conditioned checkpoint given the agent’s per-step instructions and markers. We refer to the last two settings as language guidance and visual guidance.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Short-Horizon Instruction Following. The short-horizon benchmarks test whether the guidance steers the policy. The YAM benchmark uses counterfactual instruction pairs: both instructions in a pair start from the same scene, which includes distractor objects, and differ only in the requested behavior, so a policy that repeats one plausible behavior regardless of the instruction can succeed on at most one instruction of each pair. It spans eight reference categories with three pairs each, giving 24 pairs and 48 instructions (Fig. 56). Six categories test grounding: nominal references identify objects or receptacles by name, category, or color; spatial references specify a position, relation, or distance; ordinal references select within an ordering, including relative size; cardinal references specify a number of objects or operations; arm references specify the acting arm; and exclusion references name an object that must be left untouched. Two categories test execution: action references distinguish operations such as opening versus closing, and grasp references constrain the approach or contact region. Each instruction is evaluated in three trials per setting (144 trials per setting). We report pass@1, the mean trial success, and pass@3, the fraction of instructions solved in at least one of their three trials.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: The Dexter benchmark likewise separates reference types, without counterfactual pairs, in dexterous pickand-place with colored cubes. It contains 32 tasks, each requiring the robot to move a specified cube into a specified basket with a permitted hand, grouped into four overlapping categories: attribute references (color, the Dexter counterpart of nominal references, 6 tasks), spatial references (12), ordinal references (7), and compositions of these references and constraints (9). A trial succeeds if the correct cube is released inside the specified basket by a permitted hand and remains stable for 2 s. Each task is evaluated in two trials per setting (64 trials per setting).
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Results. Tab. 22 lists every benchmark behind Fig. 8. On short-horizon tasks, visual guidance gives the highest success on both robots. On YAM, pass@1 rises from 41.7% for GR00T 2 and 55.6% with language guidance to 83.3% with visual guidance, and the gap narrows but persists at pass@3 (64.6%, 79.2%, and 89.6%). On Dexter, success rises from 29.7% and 32.8% to 70.3%. On long-horizon tasks, visual guidance completes 17 of 20 YAM trash-sorting episodes and 3 of 10 episodes of the board-disassembly stress test, whereas neither GR00T 2 nor language guidance completes any episode of either task. On Dexter trash sorting, visual guidance completes 9 of 20 episodes, against none for GR00T 2 and 1 with language guidance. Paired by layout, it sorts more items correctly than language guidance on 15 of the 20 layouts and fewer on 3 (two-sided sign test, 𝑝= 0.008).
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: The YAM category breakdown (Tab. 23) shows where visual guidance helps. It reaches 100% pass@1 on nominal, spatial, and exclusion references and 94.4% on ordinal references. Language guidance alone already helps on nominal and ordinal references (88.9% each) but barely on spatial references (from 50.0% to 55.6%), where the marked grasp or release point resolves the relation directly. Gains are smaller on the two execution categories: relative to GR00T 2, success rises from 55.6% to 72.2% on action references and from 27.8% to 55.6% on grasp references. The markers do not specify the grasp approach, object orientation, or the motion required for operations such as flipping, pouring, and scooping. On Dexter, visual guidance gains most over GR00T 2 on spatial, ordinal, and compositional tasks (50.0, 57.1, and 50.0 points) and little on attribute tasks

blocks.text: Guidance Following. Success rates alone do not show that GR00T 2 follows the guidance, because a steerable policy should change its behavior when only the guidance changes (Chen et al., 2026d). The counterfactual pairs of the YAM short-horizon benchmark are designed to test a system-level version of this: within a pair, the scene is fixed and only the requested behavior changes. Counting a pair as solved if both of its instructions succeed in at least two of three trials, GR00T 2 solves 4 of the 24 pairs (16.7%), language guidance 10 (41.7%), and visual guidance 19 (79.2%). Conversely, 24 of the 60 successful trials of GR00T 2 (40.0%) come
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: from instructions whose counterpart fails all three trials, as expected from a policy that repeats one behavior regardless of the instruction. This share falls to 12.5% (10 of 80) with language guidance and 5.8% (7 of 120) with visual guidance. On YAM trash sorting, GR00T 2 also follows the arm assignment: with visual guidance, the marked (and named) arm made 169 of 172 gripper closures (98.3%), against 164 of 181 (90.6%) for the named arm with language guidance, so wrong-arm closures fall from 9.4% to 1.7%. Its releases also follow the markers: with visual guidance, every release aimed at a bin landed in the marked bin, with one case unclear, whereas with language guidance, 21 items went into a wrong bin, or a different item was moved, after the agent had named the correct bin (see Failure Analysis).
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Agent Cost and Latency. Steering adds the agent’s cost and latency to every episode, which we measure on trash sorting on both robots (Tab. 24). With visual guidance, an episode takes a median of 9 agent turns and costs $0.26 on YAM and $0.14 on Dexter, and the robot waits for the agent during 38% and 32% of the episode. GR00T 2 was served without the accelerations of Sec. 4.6.1 on YAM (about 0.6 s per policy call) and with TensorRT on Dexter (about 0.14 s).

blocks.text: Failure Analysis. Failures on YAM trash sorting differ in kind between the two agent-guided settings. With visual guidance, 6 of 100 items are lost, in 3 episodes, and each of these episodes contains a failed hand-over, in which the agent asked one arm to stage an item at the center of the table for the other arm. By the agent’s step-end observations, every release aimed at a bin landed in the marked bin, with one case unclear. Of the 54 items lost with language guidance, 21 were released into a wrong bin, or a different item was moved, after the agent had named the correct bin, and 20 were never attempted because the agent spent the remaining steps retrieving misplaced items. On Dexter trash sorting, visual guidance leaves 11 items in a wrong bin, against 43 with language guidance and 56 for GR00T 2, while a similar share of pick-and-place attempts ends in some bin in every setting (72%, 65%, and 71%), so the settings differ mainly in choosing the right bin.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Simulation Test of Steerability on LIBERO. Simulation lets us test steerability without the agent by computing the markers from the simulator state. We evaluate 45 tasks from LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), which perturbs the scenes and instructions of LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), with 10 episodes per task (448 valid episodes), including spatial-instruction variants of a two-bowl scene on which an earlier language-only checkpoint failed, to test steering where language is weak. We compare a single-arm language-only checkpoint with a single-arm point-conditioned checkpoint, both mid-trained for 20k steps on RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), LIBERO, and DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024). This simulation checkpoint uses an earlier, richer form of the interface: a time-colored end-effector path with a disc at the next grasp or release point. The markers raise success from 69.6% (312 of 448) for the language-only checkpoint to 85.0% (381), while the same point-conditioned checkpoint with nothing drawn reaches 72.5% (325). On the two-bowl variants, the markers raise success from 18 of 70 for the language-only checkpoint (20 with nothing drawn) to 41 of 70. Across tasks, the marked checkpoint does better than the language-only checkpoint on 13, worse on 8, and ties on the other 24.
blocks.section: G.2. Agentic Steering with Visual Guidance

blocks.text: Limitations. Visual steering also has three limitations. The points specify spatial targets and the acting arm, not a manipulation strategy, which limits the gains on grasp and action references. Every step moves one arm, so coordinated two-arm motion is excluded, and a hand-over becomes two single-arm steps. On the real robots, generalization to new scenes and objects is not tested.
